title: Will the NSA "scandal" affect Digital Humanitarians and Crisis Mapping?
html:
Over the past few years, I have often found myself pondering if the eventual elimination of the flash drive through use of the cloud, NFC, Bluetooth, etc. would really help with disaster response in many ways but especially in helping to get information to/from the affected population. I was about to write a blog post about the idea when the NSA “scandal” broke.  At the same time, I was reading Eric Schmidt and Jared Cohen’s new book The New Digital Age: Reshaping the Future of People, Nations and Business which made me question if and how such privacy issues will hamper the Digital Humanitarians and Crisis Mapping in the future. Even if just out of fear.

I know that, from living in places like North Korea, the truth can be painted in very different ways when all details are not known…and that fear is an amazingly effective tool used by governments and spread by media. With full detail of the NSA activities probably quite some time away, I wonder how the current lack of information and resulting fear will cause people to back away from assisting digitally during an emergency and some of the affected population from from providing information online. Or will the little that is being released be enough to pacify ourselves and we continue to move forward? 

We already know that some fear digital volunteering for liability reasons, but will  the US government’s program that “snatches data as it passes through the fiber optic cables that make up the Internet’s backbone…..that…copies Internet traffic as it enters and leaves the United States, then routes it to the NSA for analysis”  be more than some can handle? Capturing Internet traffic that enters and leaves the United states is much broader than access to private company servers. How does it affect US-based NGOs? Or traffic to/from the UN’s servers in New York? Or a Crisis Mapper based in the Philippines working through Google Docs (in the US) to help an affected person in Pakistan who happens to be a very distant relative of a suspected terrorist in Afghanistan.  Can the US government capture that information and begin spying on the assisting person simply because s/he was trying to help?  There are many complicated cases like this one that may scare away the regular citizen.

Of course, one has to be very ignorant to think that we had complete privacy working on the Internet in the first place.  We are dealing with technology after all and I have always told my managers when they ask if something is secure that there is “always a way”. About a decade ago, I personally ran phone lines for UN VoIP phones connected to a VSAT in Pyongyang. Within days, those phone lines were tapped and centrally monitored. Anything can be done so let’s make sure that we are not completely ignorant.

However, the issue that perhaps concerns me the most yet makes me laugh at the same time is some of the things that Eric Schmit, the former Google CEO, wrote in his new book knowing full well (I suspect) what the US government was up to. He noted that “thick skin will be a necessity for technology companies in the coming years of the digital age, because they will find themselves beset by public concerns over privacy, security and user protections. It simply won’t be possible to avoid these discussions, nor will companies be able to avoid taking a position on the issues.” Yet, Google had not taken any public position on the matter until it was too late.

Schmit notes that “building the kind of system that can monitor and contain all types of dissident energy is thankfully not easy and will require very specialized solutions, expensive consultants, technologies not widely available and a  great deal of money”….yet….“everything a regime would need to build an incredibly intimidating digital police state is commercially available now, and export restrictions are currently insufficiently monitored and enforced.”. I guess he would know both from his knowledge of industry technology and the NSA programs?

He continues by noting the challenge for intelligence agencies will be how to “integrate all of their digital databases into a centralized structure so that the right dots can be connected without violating citizens’ privacy?” and that “Governments operating surveillance platforms will surely violate restrictions placed on them (by legislation or legal ruling)”. Does he ask this question because of what he knows NSA (and possibly other governments) were already doing?

But perhaps the most concerning point he makes is that “….once built, such a system will never be dismantled. Even if a dire security situation were to improve, what government would willingly give up such a powerful law-enforcement tool?” So, can we assume that even with the current uproar about the NSA programs, that these ongoing projects will continue as-is?  And, that companies like Google will continue to take a largely passive stance until these activities are made public?

I do not have a satisfactory answer to the question of what one should do or what will happen. I won’t stop using many of the tools provided by private companies outlined in the NSA scandal. But other will. Perhaps there will be a shift to new tools such as the ones that now market themselves as “NSA safe” tools like the Dropbox competitor JottaCloud from Norway.

Security and privacy will definitely prove to be touchy subject in the digital humanitarian space for the foreseeable future. I just hope that it is not so scary that it stops anyone from trying to help those who need it.

What will you do?

Andrej
